['Appeals Nos. 481 and 482 of 1966.', 'Appeals by special leave from the judgment and order, dated April 15, 1963 of the Patna High Court in Misc.', 'Judicial Cases Nos. 342 and 346 of 1954.', '165 S.T. Desai and D.N. Mukherjee, for the appellant (in both the appeals).', 'Jagadish Swarup, Solicitor General, S.K. Aiyar, R.N. Sachthey and B.D. Sharma, for the respondent (in both the appeals).', 'The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shelat, J.', 'These two appeals, under special leave, arise from two References to the High Court of Patna under section 66(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1922 and relate to the assessment years 1.945 46 and 1947.', 'In the first appeal, the question arising for determination is whether, on the facts and circumstances of the case, the surplus receipt of Rs. 13,43,469/ , realised as a result of the side of gold, is assessable as income, or profits or gains for the assessment year 1945 46 under section 4(3) (vii) of the Act.', 'In the 2nd appeal, two questions arise for determination; one relates to the surplus receipt of Rs. 33,481/ arising out of the sale of some more gold, and the second relates to the receipt of Rs. 88,522/ realised by the assessee as a receipt as a result of sale of certain shares.', 'All the three questions raise the common problem whether the said transactions in gold and shares were by way of realisation of investment or were adventures in the nature of trade or business.', 'The assessee was at all material times a landholder deriving large income from agriculture, royalties of minerals and income from forests forming part of his estate.', 'Prior to 1937, when he was a minor, his estate was under the management of a Court of Wards.', 'On attaining majority, the estate, which included Government securities of the value of about Rs. 40 lacs, was handed over to him on August 19, 1937.', 'During the account year 1938 39 he sold the whole.', 'lot of these securities and realised Rs. 44,25,088/ , the sale thus resulting in an excess of Rs. 4,55,305/ .', 'This excess amount was assessed as profit by the income tax officer for the assessment year 1939 40.', 'But on appeal against the assessment order, the Appellate Tribunal set side that order on a finding that the said sale was by way of a change in investment, and therefore, was not a transaction in the nature of trade or business.', "On March 23, 1939, the assessee opened an account in the Imperial Bank of India initially with Rs. 46 lacs, which included the said sale proceeds of Rs. 44 lacs 'and odd and to which on March 27, 1939 he added Rs. 2.60 lacs.", 'The account was opened in the name of his wife and was called "Account of Rs. 48 lacs floating in the share market \' \' \' In September 1939, the assessee purchased shares and debentures of the value of Rs. 34.14 lacs from out of the funds in the said account.', 'He, however, sold certain shares for Rs. 5,75,723/ in October 1939, and then the rest of them in 1940 and 1941 realising Rs. 29,58,677/ and 166 Rs. 64,201/ respectively.', 'The first sale fetched a proFit of Rs. 1,17,064/ the second a profit of Rs. 25,133 and the third a loss of Rs. 1,642/ .', 'The income tax officer brought to tax the two surpluses in the assessments for the assessment years 1940 41 and 1941 42.', "But the department was again unsuccessful as the Tribunal once again held, on the strength of the correspondence which had passed between the assessee, his bankers axed his brokers in Calcutta, that the only possible conclusion emerging from that correspondence was that the assessee 's intention was not to deal in shares and debentures, and that the said transactions were a mere change in investment carried out of a single scheme of earning a better yield from investments.", "The Tribunal 's orders in respect of these assessments for the assessment years 1939 40 to 1941 42 were made part of the Statement of Case filed by the Tribunal be,fore the High Court in the present References.", 'Between June 28, 1940 and November 9, 1940 the assessee purchased 68,109 tolas of gold for Rs. 28,47,380/ from out of the sale proceeds of the said shares.', 'The gold so purchased was kept in his family vaults at Padma, the seat of his estate, for nearly 4 years.', 'Between October 9, 1944 and October 20, 1944, he disposed of the bulk of the gold, i.e. 55,494 tolas, for Rs. 36,80,174/ , the sale resulting in a surplus of Rs. 13,43,469/ , which is the subject matter of the first appeal.', 'The remaining quantity of gold was sold of October 19, 1945, and that sale brought_ him an excess of Rs. 33,481/ , which is part of the subject matter of the second appeal.', 'In respect of these two surplus amounts, the assessee contended that they were the result of a change in investment and could not be said to be transactions in the nature of trade or business.', "His case was that neither the Government securities, nor the shares and debentures purchased out of their sale proceeds, nor the gold were sold and purchased by way of dealing in them, that at no time they became his stock in trade for any business or adventures in the nature of trade or business therein, that the transactions were mere conversions from one investment to another, depending upon the circumstances which prevailed during the respective periods and that the sale of gold in 1944 and 1945 was occasioned partly due to the tide in the second world war turning in favour of the ,allies and partly due (a) to his having to pay Rs. 7 lacs by way of income tax, (b) expenses for the marriage of his younger brother, (c) for payment of Rs. 6 lacs debt to one Gupta and (d) for purchase of Victory Bonds worth Rs. 14 lacs and odd 'at the instance of the Government authorities as contribution of his estate to the war effort.", 'The Tribunal rejected the case that gold had been sold for the reasons given by the assessee or as a change in investment and 167 held that: (1 ) conversion of shares into gold was not due to any panic resulting from the war, (2) that there was no pressing necessity for the sale of gold as alleged by him, (3) that Victory Bonds were not by way of any war effort since the assessee sold them away within a short time after their purchase, and (4) that he sale proceeds of gold were utilised in purchasing shares for which he borrowed an additional amount of Rs. 5.10 lacs in 1945 46 against gold.', "in this view the Tribunal confirmed the I.T.O. 's decision that the two excess amounts were liable to income tax in the two assessment years.", 'The sale proceeds of gold sold as aforesaid were utilised by the assessee in purchasing 7(325 shares of Karanpura Development Co. Ltd. for Rs. 2,37,267/ during the period from December 8, 1944 to April 20, 1945 and shares of Bokaro Ramgur Co. for Rs. 39,81,663/ purchased in 1945 46.', "Part of the sale proceeds were 'also.", 'utilised in purchasing the said Victory Bonds.', 'between November 8, 1945 and February 21, 1946, he sold 6950 of the Karanpura shares realising a net surplus of Rs. 88,522/ , which the Income Tax Officer treated as business profit and brought to tax for the assessment year 1946 47.', "As the Statement of Case by the Tribunal shows, the Tribunal examined the assessee 's dealings since the time he took over the said estate.", 'The Tribunal noted that the said shares were purchased from the said Rs. 48 lacs in the Bank reserved ,for that purpose and that they were sold and purchased at very short intervals.', 'From these facts it held that he must be considered to have launched a scheme in dealing in shares, which conclusion, it thought, was strengthened by the fact of the assessee having borrowed Rs. 5.10 lacs for the said purpose.', "The Tribunal further held that the complete picture of the said transactions over a length of time had not 'been before the preceding Tribunal when it passed the earlier orders for the assessment years 1939 40 to 1941 42, and therefore, its conclusions were not applicable to the transactions in question.", 'It consequently held the assessee to be a dealer in shares.', "As regards the gold ,also, the Tribunal confirmed the orders of the I.T.O. rejecting the assessee 's case that the gold was purchased by him owing to the war crisis and sold by him on account of the pressing necessities alleged by him and the change in the war situation then.", 'By an order dated April 2, 1959, the High Court referred that statement of Case back to the Tribunal under section 66(4) directing it to consider further all the materials before it and file a supplementary Statement of Case as the High Court found the Statement factually incorrect in certain respects.', 'The Tribunal accordingly sent a supplementary Statement of Case on April 23, 1960.', "After setting out the assessees transactions of the sale of Government securities in 1938 39, the purchase of shares from 168 their sale proceeds, their sale in 1939 40 and 1940 41, the purchase of gold 'and its sale, the Tribunal once again rejected the assessee 's claim that those transactions were conversions of one investment to another made for a better return or that the gold was sold in October 1944 for pressing necessities alleged by the assessee.", "Regarding the purchase and sale of shares, the Tribunal stated that the assessee purchased shares of the value of Rs. 37 lacs and odd in1945 46, that those were shares of two, concerns only, Bokaro, and Ramgur Co. Ltd. and Karanpura Development Co. Ltd. and that as the latter company 's shares were of the value of Rs. 2,37,267/ only, the 'bulk of the amount of Rs. 37 lacs and odd went into the purchase of the shares of Bokaro: and Ramgur Co. Ltd. The Tribunal noted that the sale of Karanpura shares resulted in a net profit of Rs. 88,522/ , that in respect of the Karanpura shares there was correspondence showing that his brokers had advised him to acquire 51% of the company 's share holding as he desired to obtain control over its management, that for doing so he wanted to obtain founders ' shares (each of which shares carried 3 votes per share), that a compromise was proposed in a suit he had filed as the lessor of the mines leased out to the company, that M/s. Bird & Co., the managing agents of that company, were not willing to.", "sell him shares representing the unissued capital of the company on terms proposed by the assessee and that ultimately he failed to obtain majority of shares which only could have enabled him to obtain control over the company 's management.", 'But the Tribunal found that "the assessee was attempting to obtain control of the company not by purchasing of shares in the market, but by issue of shares by the company in order to settle the dispute between the company and the assesses These negotiations finally failed.', '" It finally held that having perused the correspondence and having regard to the circumstances, the purchase of Karanpura shares was not in pursuance of a scheme to obtain control over the company by acquiring 51% of the votes therein.', "The High Court, after hearing the: References, held that though the Tribunal had in the earlier assessments held that the assessee 's transactions in shares, securities and gold did not amount to transactions in the nature of trade or business, and therefore, the assessee could not be treated as a dealer in those articles.", 'There was no bar to the revenue coming to a different conclusion, though to do so it must have some new materials and facts before it.', "It further held that the present Tribunal could a/so arrive at such a conclusion having regard to: (a) the frequency of transactions of purchase and sale of shares, (b) the short interval between purchase and sale of shares, (c) the fact of Rs. 48 lacs in the assessee 's wife 's account having been ear marked for shares transactions, (d) his borrowing Rs. 5.10 lacs 'against gold for purchase 169 of shares, and lastly, the fact that the Tribunal this time had before it a more complete picture of the assessee 's transactions over a length of period which its predecessor had not when it dealt with the assessments for the assessment years 1939 40 to 1941 42.", 'The High Court further held that there was fresh material, namely, that when the gold was sold, its sale proceeds were again invested in shares and the fact that though Victory Bonds were purchased in January 1945 they were sold after an interval of two months only.', 'The High Court, in this view, concluded that "the Appellate.', 'Tribunal, therefore had before it fresh materials for coming to a conclusion contrary to the one come by its predecessors in the previous orders.', '" It rejected the assessee \'s case: (a) that he had converted one investment into another, i.e. from shares and securities to gold, because of the worsening of the war situation after the fall of France in 1940, (b) that when the war situation improved in 1944 and with that the price of gold began to fail he once again converted his investment from gold to shares, i.e., from an unproductive investment into one which could give him an adequate yield, and (c) that he had sold gold because of pressing necessities.', "The first contention was held unsustainable because even after purchasing gold the assessee had retained considerable cash; the second was rejected on the ground that the assessee had sold gold not because of the allied victory in sight but because he found the gold unprofitabIe by reason of the fall in its price and the third was rejected as the assessee had failed to make_good the pressing necessities alleged ' by him.", "The High Court further held that the findings given by the Appellate Tribunal were all findings of fact and as they could not be said to have been arrived at without any evidence they could not be interfered with in a Reference under section 66(2), and answered the questions as to the two surplus amounts of Rs. 13 lacs and odd and Rs. 33 thousand 'and odd as liable to assessment.", "In regard to the excess of Rs. 88,522/_ resulting from the sale of ' Karanpura shares, the High Court agreed with the Tribunal that that amount also was rightly brought to tax.", "It held that the finding of the Tribunal that the purchase of these shares was not in pursuance of a scheme to obtain control in the company and that the assessee 's scheme for that purpose was to acquire shares representing the unissued capital of the company was one of fact with which also it had no jurisdiction to interfere.", "Counsel for the appellant disputed the correctness of the High Court 's judgment and contended: (1 ) that it was in error in declining to go into the correctness of the findings of the Tribunal by merely stating that they were findings of fact, (2) that the question whether a particular item was a trading profit or capital accretion depended on the intention on the part of the assessee at the time of the transaction in question and which had Sup CI/70 12 170 to be arrived at by an inference from established facts and was, therefore, a mixed question of fact and law, (3) that on the facts and circumstances, the Tribunal, and following it the High Court, was in error in treating the gold and the Karanpura shares as the stock in trade of the assessee for his alleged trading activities, (4) that the onus of proving that the activities of the assessee amounted to activities in the nature of trade or business was on the department and particularly so,, as the Tribunal in the earlier assessments had come to a contrary conclusion, and (5) that the facts and circumstances as accepted by the Tribunal in its Statement of Case showed that the purchases of gold and share were made without any intention at that time to resell them at profit, and that therefore, the subsequent sales thereof would not stamp those transactions with the character of trade or business in them.", 'Since these appeals arise out of References under section 66(2), we cannot exercise any wider power of interference than that permitted to the High Court under the Act.', 'That was not disputed by Mr. Desai.', "But in support of his contention that this was a case ' where the High Court could and should have interfered with the Tribunal 's findings he cited a number of decisions.", 'It is not necessary to go into all these decisions as the principles on which such interference can be made and the scope of power under section 66 to do so are by now well established.', 'That the question, whether an assessee carries on business or whether certain transactions are in the course of business or whether they amount to adventures in the nature of trade or business, is a mixed question of fact and law is well settled.', 'The decision in Venkataswami Naidu & Co. vs', "T.(1) is an instance in point where this Court observed that the expression 'adventure in the nature of trade ' appearing in the definition of 'business ' implies the existence of certain elements in the .adventure which in law would invest it with the character of trade and that renders the question whether a transaction 'is in the nature of trade a mixed question of law and fact and the High Court in such a case would interfere if the Tribunal had misdirected itself in law of 'also Liquidators of Pursa Ltd. rs.", 'C.I.T.)(2).', 'But to distinguish a question of fact and a question of law is not always easy, for, sometimes there is a common area between the two and though a mere question of fact can be turned into one of law, care should be taken against a finding of a mixed question of fact and law being given the unassailability which the Act confers on a pure finding of fact.', 'The case of Sree Menakshi Mills Ltd. vs', 'T.(3) holds that where an ultimate finding on an issue is an inference to be drawn from facts found, on application of a principle of law, there is a mixed question of law and fact and such an inference in such a (1) at 603 to 604.', '(2) (3) 171 case is a question of law open to review by the court.', 'On the other hand, when the final determination of the issue does not involve any application of a principle of law, an inference is a pure inference of fact drawn from the other basic facts.', 'Such an inference can be attacked only if there is no evidence to support it, or, if it is perverse.', "Since the expression 'adventure in the nature of trade ' implies the existence of certain elements in the transactions which in law would invest them with the character of trade or business and the question on that account becomes a mixed question of law and fact, the Court can review the Tribunal 's finding if it has misdirected itself in law.", 'It is fairly clear that where a person in selling his investment realises an enhanced price, the excess over his purchase price is not profit assessable to tax But it would be so, if what is done is not a mere realisation of the investment but an act done for making profits.', 'The distinction between the two types of transactions is not always easy to make The distinction whether the transaction is of one kind or the other depends on the question whether the excess was an enhancement of the value by realising a security or a gain in an operation of profit making.', "If the transaction is in the ordinary line of the 'assessee 's business there would hardly be any difficulty in concluding that it was a trading transaction, but where it is not, the facts must be properly assessed to discover whether it was in the nature of trade.", 'The surplus realised on the sale of shares, for instance, would be capital if the assessee is an ordinary investor realising his holding; but it would be revenue, if he deals with them as an adventure in the nature of trade.', 'The fact that the original purchase was made with the intention to resell if an enhanced price could be obtained is by itself not enough but in conjunction with the conduct of the assessee and other circumstances it may point to the trading character of the transaction.', "For instance, an 'assessee may invest his capital in shares with the intention to resell them if in future their sale may bring in higher price.", 'Such an investment, though motivated by a possibilty of enhanced value, does not render the investment a transaction in the nature of trade.', 'The test often applied is, has the assessee made his shares and securities the stock in trade of a business.', 'Though the assessee was at the material time a landholder of a large estate, that fact by itself would not mean that his transactions in shares, securities and bullion cannot be transactions in the nature of trade.', 'They had, therefore, to be examined in the light of all the facts and circumstances to ascertain whether they had been entered into in pursuit of a trading activity.', 'The first relevant ,fact iS that the assessees occupation was that of a landholder, having, on attaining majority, a considerable amount of money available for raising income therefrom.', 'The transactions 172 in question were obviously not in the line of any business or trade carried on by him.', "Since the Tribunal came to a conclusion as regards the nature of the assessee 's transactions different from that arrived at earlier, it would be useful to tabulate them at one place.", 'So tabulated, they are as follows: (1) Sale of Government securities in 1938 39 which realised Rs. 44.25 lacs; (2) Opening of an account with this and certain other amounts totaling Rs. 48 lacs in the Imperial Bank; (3) Purchase out of these funds, shares and debentures of the value of Rs. 34.14 lacs in September 1939; (4) Sale in October 1939, i.e., within a month, of some of these shares bringing him Rs. 5.75 lacs; (5) Sale of the bulk of the shares in 1940 bringing in Rs. 29.58 lacs; (6) Sale of the remaining shares in 1941 resulting in a small deficit; (7) Purchase of 68,109 tolas of gold in June 1940 for Rs. 28.47 lacs; (8) Sale of the bulk of the gold, i.e., 55,495 tolas in October 1944 resulting in a surplus of Rs. 13 lacs and odd; (9) Sale of the remaining gold in October 1945 resulting in a surplus cf Rs. 33,481/ ; (10) Purchase of Karanpura shares between December 1944 and April 1945 of the value of Rs. 2,37,267/ ; (11 ) Purchase of Victory Bonds in January 1945 of Rs. 14 lacs, and sale thereof in March 1945; (12) Borrowing Rs. 5.10 lacs against gold in 1945 46; (13) Purchase of Bokaro Ramgur shares in 1945 46 for Rs. 39.81 lacs and (14) Sale of Karanpura shares in 1945 46 bringing in a surplus of Rs. 88,000 and odd.', 'As already stated, though these transactions were not in the line of any trade of business carried on by the assessee, nonetheless, if they possess the characteristics of adventures in the nature of trade, the profits resulting therefrom would be liable to tax.', 'But in an enquiry on the question whether these transactions were in the nature of trade or business, it would not be altogether irrelevant 173 to notice that in 1938 39, when the assessee sold the Government securities, he sold the entire lot and invested the bulk of their sale proceeds in shares and debentures, i.e., as much as Rs. 34 lacs.', 'The same features is present also in his purchase of gold in 1940 and its disposal in 1944 and 1945 using its sale proceeds in buying shares, which, it must be remembered, were of two companies only.', 'The transactions thus are not diversified nor are gradual according to the opportunities offered by fluctuating market prices, but are in bulk and almost at a time, which ordinarily are not the characteristics of the dealings of a person carrying on trade or business in them.', 'Thus, in 1938 39 all Government securities were sold and the bulk of their sale proceeds, i.e. Rs. 34 lacs and odd, used in the purchase of shares.', "The same was the case when gold was bought 'and sold.", 'Furthermore, when a person trades in shares and debentures, he does not ordinarily buy shares of two companies only, except when a particular script has the possibility of giving an unusual or a certain profit.', 'There was nothing on record to show, nor did the Tribunal find, that that was the case with the shares of either of the two companies whose shares the assessee purchased in such large quantity.', 'Prima facie these transactions would appear in the nature of investments and their conversion into what the assessee believed to be better investments as the circumstances changed from time to time.', 'In support of his contention that these transactions were not in the nature of trade or business, the assessee had relied on the correspondence between him on the one hand and his bankers and brokers on the other, which had satisfied the Tribunal previously with reference to the assessment years 1939 40 to 1941 42.', "That correspondence lends support to the assessee 's case inasmuch as he had there in clearly instructed his brokers to invest the sale proceeds of the said Government securities in such a way as to give him an annual yield of net 7%.", 'There can be no doubt that Government securities were sold accordingly and shares of certain companies were purchased from their sale proceeds in accordance with the advice of his brokers and bankers.', 'When it was found that certain shares so purchased were not Likely to yield the percentage he desired, they were sold within hardly a month from their purchase.', "The circumstances in which these transactions were brought 'about, would disclose, as was held by the previous Tribunal in the case of the earlier assessments, that the assessee 's intention then was to change his investments from Government securities into shares and debentures which, he was advised, would procure him a better yield.", "This conclusion is consistent with his sale of the entire lot of Government securities 'at 'a time, his going in for shares with their sale proceeds and the sale in October 1939 of certain shares which were found incapable of giving the return he desired.", "174 Since the present Tribunal had the advantage of examining the assessee 's transactions during the whole of the period, i.e., right from 1938 39 to 1944 45 and thus have a more comprehensive picture of all the transactions, there would be no bar to its coming to a conclusion different from that arrived at in the earlier years, if the acts and conduct of the assessee taken as a whole throughout the period pointed to ,a different conclusion as both the Tribunal and the High Court have said.", 'But the only new materials pointed out by the Tribunal from which a different conclusion could be arrived at were (1) the sale of gold in 1944 and 1945, (2) the purchase of the said shares from its sale proceeds, and (3) the sale of Karanpura shares.', 'The question, therefore, the Tribunal had before it was, whether when the assessee purchased the gold he did so with the intention to deal in it.', "The Tribunal held, and the High Court concurred with it, that the assessee 's transactions showed that they were in the nature of trading transactions.", 'Two facts, however, throw considerable doubt on the validity of that conclusion and neither the Tribunal nor the High Court seems to have weighed them with the consideration which they demand.', 'The first fact is that in 1940 he converted his entire share holding into gold, a fact consistent with his case that he did so because of the nervousness engendered by the breaking out of the Second World War, the initial German victories and the fall of France.', 'The Tribunal did not countenance this case for it thought that if that was so, the assessee would have invested the other cash lying with him also in gold, and secondly because according to it the war panic started in 1942 and not in 1940.', "We do not think that this was an accurate 'approach.", 'The fact that the assessee did not invest all his cash cannot mean, as the Tribunal thought, that his case about the purchase of gold was not correct.', 'The war had commenced in 1939 and it is a notorious fact that in 1940 the fortunes of the allies were none too bright.', 'The fact was that the assessee sold his entire share holding and applied their sale proceeds and also a further amount of Rs. 13 lacs and odd obtained ,from his lessees, M/s Anderson Wright & Co., into.', 'The second fact, whose significance does not also seem to have been adequately apprehended, was that the assessee, who started with the plan of getting at least net 7% yield, put a very Large part of his funds into gold, an altogether sterile security, and retained that gold in his family vaults ,for nearly 4 years.', 'The Tribunal had before it the gold prices current during the years 1940 to 1944.', 'These indicate that the gold price remain steady at Rs. 42 per tola all throughout 1940.', 'There was, however, an upward trend noticeable from about the end of 1941 which went up to Rs. 65 towards the end of 1942.', 'By the middle of 1943 the gold price had risen to Rs. 90 and even more.', 'In October 1944, when the assessee sold 175 a large bulk of his gold holding the price was at Rs. 68 per tolaIf the idea of the assessee in purchasing the gold was to trade in it, he would not have waited for 4 years without disposing of a particle of it.', 'The price was on the upward trend in 1941 and reached the climax in 1943 when he could have sold the gold and made considerable gain.', "The fact that he did not do so and waited until October 1944 the war fortunes were turning in favour of ' the allies, that confidence had gradually been regained by trading circles and that that was why he thought that it was no longer necessary for him to retain the ,gold any further and could safely invest his money in income bearing securties.", 'The further fact that he sold practically the whole of his stock of gold in October 1944 instead of selling it bit by bit when the price was rising since about the end of 1942 is inconsistent with the hypothesis that the object with which the gold was purchased was to trade in it.', 'Regarding share transactions, we think that the Tribunal placed undue emphasis on the fact that when he opened the bank account in March 1939 with the sale proceeds of Government securities, he did so, firstly, in the name of his wife \'and, secondly, called that account as one of "Rs. 48 lacs floating in the share \' market".', 'The first had no particular significance and the second properly viewed only meant that he wanted to set apart this fund for transactions in shares and securities and not mix up his other capital and the income arising from his estate.', "The name he gave ' to this account cannot for that reason only render his dealing with that account into trading transactions if otherwise, they were not.", 'Similarly, the Tribunal was unduly impressed by the fact that he sold away the Victory Bonds within about two months from their purchase.', 'The correspondence produced by the assessee clearly shows that he had bought those Bonds at the pressure of the then Commissioner.', 'The Bonds were not likely to fetch him the yield he desired.', 'His purchase of them had thus served the purpose, viz., his showing to the authorities that his estate had made a war contribution.', 'The sale by him of those Bonds would not affect the Government or its war effort.', "The fact that he sold ' them soon after the purchase would not invest it with the stamp of ' trade or business in Victory Bonds.", "As regards the Karanpura shares, the correspondence between him and the company and the advice he had from his brokers referred to in the Statement of Case show that the assessee did at one time entertain the idea of obtaining control over the company 's management by procuring 51% of its total shares.", 'He could do so by purchasing shares in the open market and also, by other means.', 'He purchased 7,025 shares in the market but that ,was clearly not enough.', 'There was at that time litigation going on_ 176 between him and the company and he seems to have hit upon the idea that he would compromise his suit if the managing agents of the company were to sell him shares representing its unissued capital at prices offered by him.', "The object of his offer was that he would not have to pay the market price of the shares which was 3 times more than the one offered 'by him.", 'The company did not agree and his move for compromise ,failed.', 'According to him, there was, therefore, no useful purpose for retaining those shares and he sold 6,950 shares leaving only 75 shares with him.', 'On these facts the Tribunal was not right in concluding that the shares which the assessee purchased from the market were not for the purpose of acquiring the major share holding in the company and that the control over the company was to be obtained only by purchasing shares representing the unissued capital.', "Both the purchase of shares and the move to obtain shares representing the unissued capital were part of the same design and if the latter 'failed, his purchase of 7,025 shares would obviously not bring him nearer his object.", 'Furthermore, the bulk of the sale proceeds of gold went into the purchase of Bokaro.', 'Ramgur shares which remained with him till the assessment years in question.', "The profits made on the sale of shares, acquired with the intention of obtaining control over the company 's management and not for dealing in them, would be on the capital and not revenue account.", '(see Kishan Prasad & Co. Ltd.', 'C.I.T.(1) and C.I.T. vs National Finance Ltd. (2).', "The Statement of Case itself set out facts which were consistent with the assessee 's case.", 'In our view the Tribunal misdirected itself in applying the law to the facts ,found by it both in the matter of gold and shares, and the High Court would have been entitled to interfere with its findings instead of holding that it could not do so as the findings were findings of fact.', "The questions involved being mixed questions of fact and law, the hypothesis on which the High Court acted that the findings were purely findings of fact and therefore 'were unassailable was in our view not correct.", 'The appeals, therefore, will have to be allowed and the answers given by the High Court set aside.', "We hold that the two questions referred to the High Court should have been answered in assessee 's favour and we do s0 accordingly.", 'The respondent will pay to the appellant costs of these appeals but only one hearing fee.', '(3.C. Appeal allowed.']
output: ['The assessee inherited a vast estate consisting of agricultural and other land as also Government securities worth Rs. 40 lacs.', 'In 1937 he attained majority and control of the estate from the Court of Wards.', 'In the accounting year 1938 39 he sold some of these securities at a profit.', 'Thereafter he opened an account in the Imperial Bank of India in the name of his wife and called it "account of 48 lacs floating in the share market.', '" In September 1939 he purchased shares worth Rs. 34.14 lacs out of the said fund but sold them, again at a profit in the Years 1939 \', 1940 \' and 1941.', 'The profits on the said sales of shares were subjected to tax by the Income tax Officer in the years 1939 40, 1940 41 and 1941 42.', "The Tribunal however held that the asessee was not a dealer in shares anti ' held the profits not to be taxable.", 'Between June.', 'and November 1940 the assessee purchased gold for Rs. 28.47,380/ from out of the sale proceeds of the aforesaid shares.', "This gold was sold 'at a profit in the accounting periods relevant t0 the 1945 46 and 1946 47 assessment years.", 'With the sale proceeds certain shares including 7,025 shares of Karanpura Development Co. Ltd. were purchased, most of which were sold at a profit.', 'Certain Victory Bonds were purchased and resold within two months.', 'The Income tax Officer subjected the profits from the sales of gold and Karanpur shares to tax in the assessment years 1945 46 and 1946 47.', "The Tribunal on ,considering the whole pattern of transactions from 1938 onwards came to the conclusion that the said ' profits were rightly taxed.", 'The High Court upheld the view of the Tribunal holding inter alia, that the findings were of fact and not arrived at without evidence so that no interference was warranted in reference proceedings.', 'The assessee appealed.', "HELD: (1) When a transaction is not in the ordinary lines of an assessee 's business the facts must be properly assessed to discover whether it was in the nature of trade.", "The test often applied ' is has the assessee made his shares and securities the stock in trade of a business ? [171 G; 172 H] (ii) Since in the present case the Tribunal had the advantage of examining the assessee 's transactions during the whole period i.e. right from 1938 39 to 1944 45 and thus had more comprehensive picture of all the transactions, there would be no bar to its coming to a conclusion different from that arrived at in the earlier years.", 'if the acts and conduct of the assessee taken as a whole throughout the period pointed to a different conclusion.', '[174 A B] (iii) On the facts and circumstances of the case, however the finding of the Tribunal, concurred in by the High Court, that the transactions in question were in the nature of trading transactions, was not justified.', '[174 C D] 164 (a) It is a notorious fact that in 1940 the fortunes of the allies were none too bright.', 'The conversion by the assessee of his entire share holding into gold in that year was consistent with his case that he did so because of the nervousness engendered by the breaking out of the war, the initial German victories, and the fall of France.', "The fact that the assessee did not invest all his cash would not mean, 'as the Tribunal thought, that his case about the purchases of go1d was not correct.", '[174 D F] The Tribunal also failed to give due significance.', "to the fact that the assessee who started with the plan of getting 'at least net 7% yield, put a very large part of his funds into gold, an altogether sterile security, and retained it for 4 years.", 'The price of gold began to rise in 1941 and was at its peak in 1943.', 'The fact that the assessee did not sell his gold then but only in October 1944 when the price had fallen showed that it was only after the: fortunes of war had turned in favour of the allies and confidence restored that he felt it safe to invest his money in income beating securities.', 'The further fact that he sold practically the whole of his stock of gold in October 1944 instead of reselling it bit by bit after the price was rising since 1942 was inconsistent with the hypothesis that the object with which the go1d was purchased was to trade in it.', '[174 G H; 175 A D] (b) The fact that the account in the Imperial Bank opened in 1939 was called "Rs. 48 lacs floating in the share market" was given undue significance by the Tribunal.', 'Properly viewed it only meant that the assessee wanted to set apart this fund for transactions in shares and securities and not mix up his other capital and the income arising from his estate.', '[175 D E] (c) The sale of the.', 'Victory Bonds within two months of their purchase would not invest the transaction with the stamp of trade or business they were only purchased to show to the authorities that his estate had made a contribution to the war effort.', "[175] (d) The Karanpur shares were purchased by the assessee with a view to getting control over the company 's management by procuring 51% of its total shares.", 'When that plan failed he sold these shares.', 'In these circumstances the transaction could not be considered to be on revenue account.', '[175 G H; 176 D] Kishan Prasad & Co. Ltd.', 'C.I.T., and C.I.T.v.', "National Finance Ltd. , 'applied.", "(e) The expression 'adventure in the nature of trade ' implies the existence of certain elements in the transactions which in law would invest them with the character of trade or business.", 'The question therefore whether a particular transaction is an adventure.', "in the nature of trade is a mixed question of law and fact and the court can review the Tribunal 's finding thereon.", "Therefore in the present case the High Court was wrong in treating the Tribunal 's decision as a finding of fact and refusing to interfere on that ground.", '[171 A C] Venkataswami Naidu & Co.', 'C.I.T., , 603, 604 and Liquidators of Pursa Ltd. vs', 'C.I.T., , referred to.']

instruction: Answer the following Indian legal question.
input: Explain the concept of 'adverse possession' and its relationship to the Limitation Act, 1963, providing examples of its application in rural India.
output:
**Adverse Possession and Its Relationship with the Limitation Act, 1963 in Rural India**

**Adverse Possession Explained:**
Adverse possession is a legal concept where an individual gains ownership of a property that they possess and use without the owner's consent, provided they meet specific criteria over a set period. Typically, this requires uninterrupted and continuous possession for a period of either ten years or twelve years, depending on the jurisdiction, along with an assertion of ownership during this period.

**Interaction with the Limitation Act, 1963:**
The Limitation Act of 1963 in India establishes a statute of limitations for property claims. It prescribes a timeframe within which any person must initiate legal action to assert ownership or rights over property. Adverse possession often interacts with this Act because successful claims often require establishing uninterrupted possession for the required period. The Act also sets the timeframe within which the true owner can challenge such claims, usually within the statutory period.

**Application in Rural India:**
In rural areas of India, land disputes are common, and adverse possession can sometimes help individuals acquire property rights through long-term possession. For example, a person might move into a house or start farming on land without the owner's permission, asserting ownership after the possession period has elapsed.

**Example Scenario:**
Ann Sapphire moves into a house in a rural village in Haryana without the owner's consent. After living there for ten years, she claims ownership under the adverse possession doctrine. The original owner, Rahul Sharma, might challenge her claim, arguing he had no knowledge of her possession. The court would evaluate factors such as Ann's uninterrupted occupation, her assertion of ownership, and whether Rahul had any notice or legal challenge within the permissible timeframe as per the Limitation Act.

**Considerations:**
- Recent legal reforms in India, especially those focusing on women's property rights, may affect how adverse possession is applied, especially in cases where property rights were historically held by male family members.
- Cultural and customary practices in rural communities may influence how such disputes are resolved, often through mediation or community councils, rather than formal legal proceedings.

In summary, adverse possession, when successfully claimed, can allow individuals in rural India to gain legal ownership after meeting the specified criteria, relating closely to the Limitation Act's timeframe for asserting claims.

instruction: Answer the following Indian legal question.
input: Ms. Priya, residing in Mumbai, wants to sue Mr. Rajesh, residing in Kolkata, for breach of contract which was entered into in Chennai. Where can Ms. Priya file the suit under the CPC?
output:
Ms. Priya, residing in Mumbai, wants to sue Mr. Rajesh, residing in Kolkata, for breach of contract which was entered into in Chennai. Under the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC), the key considerations are jurisdiction, venue, and the concept of lis pendens.

1. **Sections 28, 29, and 30 of CPC**:
   - These sections deal with the jurisdiction of the court, the venue of suits, and other procedural aspects.
   - Section 29(1) states that any suit may be instituted in any court having jurisdiction.
   - Section 29(2) allows the court to refuse to proceed if the case could be more conveniently heard elsewhere.

2. **Key Considerations**:
   - The contract was entered into in Chennai, but Mr. Rajesh is in Kolkata and Ms. Priya is in Mumbai.
   - The suit can be filed in any court that has jurisdiction over the defendant (Mr. Rajesh) as per Section 29 of CPC.

instruction: Answer the following Indian legal question.
input: Discuss the ethical implications of 'cross-examination' and the limits an advocate should adhere to in India.
output:
**Answer**

Cross-examination is a fundamental aspect of legal practice, crucial for the integrity and fairness of the judicial system. In India, advocates play a pivotal role in upholding these principles. Here is an organized presentation of the ethical implications and the limits that advocates should adhere to:

### Ethical Implications in Indian Advocacy

1. **Professionalism and Responsibility**:  
   Advocates must uphold the integrity of the judicial system, ensuring that cross-examination is conducted with fairness and respect. This commitment to truth and justice is essential for maintaining public trust and the professional standing of the legal community.

2. **Fairness and Due Process**:  
   Cross-examination should be respectful and equitable, providing equal opportunities for both parties.Judicial rulings such as the Bombay High Court's decisions on 'cumulative truth' and the 'chaitanya combine case' emphasize the need for responsible cross-examination practices to prevent misuse and ensure procedural fairness.

3. **Avoiding Misuse**:  
   Advocates must refrain from using cross-examination for personal gain or to degrade court dignity. This includes avoiding unnecessary questions, leading witnesses, or attempting to influence the judge, which can damage credibility and integrity.

4. **Necessity and Proportionality**:  
   Cross-examination should be used judiciously. Excessive or unnecessary aggression can harm a case and diminish an advocate's credibility.

### Limits and Boundaries of Advocacy

1. **Respect for Law and Judicial Processes**:  
   Advocates must adhere to legal frameworks, including rules on cross-examination scope and manner as set by judicial councils and the Bar Council of India.

2. **Maintaining Dignity and Decorum**:  
   The practice of law demands the highest standards of professionalism. Advocates should conduct themselves with dignity and decorum, both within and outside the courtroom.

3. **Limits During Cross-Examination**:  
   Specific limits apply, including avoiding improper tactics, respecting the judge, and refraining from disrespectful behavior towards the legal process.

4. **Ethical Guidelines and Professional Standards**:  
   Bar associations and the judiciary enforce ethical guidelines and professional standards. Non-compliance can lead to disciplinary actions, reputational damage, and a tarnished career.

### Conclusion

Cross-examination's proper conduct is vital for maintaining justice and judicial integrity. By adhering to ethical guidelines and respecting legal frameworks, advocates ensure that cross-examination serves its purpose effectively, without undermining the justice system or court dignity.

instruction: Answer the following Indian legal question.
input: What kind of recommendations can the Commission make in their reports regarding measures for effective implementation of safeguards and protection, welfare, and socio-economic development of Scheduled Castes?
output:
The Commission can make a wide range of recommendations in their reports to ensure the effective implementation of safeguards, protection, welfare, and socio-economic development of Scheduled Castes. These recommendations can be broadly categorized as follows:

**1. Strengthening Legal and Constitutional Safeguards:**

*   **Legislative Reforms:** Recommending amendments to existing laws or enactment of new legislation to strengthen the safeguards provided to Scheduled Castes, address loopholes, and ensure stricter penalties for violations of their rights. This could include strengthening the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, and related legislations.
*   **Enhanced Enforcement Mechanisms:** Recommending measures to improve the enforcement of existing laws and safeguards. This could involve strengthening law enforcement agencies, special police units, and prosecution mechanisms to ensure effective investigation and conviction in cases of atrocities and discrimination against Scheduled Castes.
*   **Judicial Reforms:** Recommending measures to expedite justice delivery in cases related to Scheduled Castes, including setting up special courts, fast-track courts, and ensuring sensitization of the judiciary towards issues of caste discrimination and atrocities.

**2. Enhancing Protection from Discrimination and Atrocities:**

*   **Preventive Measures:** Recommending proactive measures to prevent atrocities and discrimination, such as community policing initiatives, awareness campaigns targeting societal attitudes and promoting social harmony, and sensitization programs for government officials, law enforcement, and judiciary on issues of caste discrimination.
*   **Victim Support and Rehabilitation:** Recommending comprehensive support systems for victims of atrocities and discrimination, including immediate relief, adequate compensation, rehabilitation programs, legal aid, psychological counseling, and witness protection.
*   **Addressing Systemic Discrimination:** Recommending measures to tackle systemic discrimination in various sectors like employment, education, housing, and public services. This could include stricter enforcement of anti-discrimination laws, affirmative action policies, and promoting inclusive practices in institutions.
*   **Social Justice and Equality Promotion:** Recommending programs and policies to promote social justice and equality, challenge caste-based prejudices and stereotypes, and foster a more inclusive and equitable society. This could involve promoting inter-caste dialogue, supporting social reform movements, and integrating social justice education in curricula.

**3. Promoting Welfare and Access to Basic Amenities:**

*   **Improved Access to Education:** Recommending measures to enhance access to quality education for Scheduled Castes at all levels, including increased scholarships, residential schools, remedial coaching, infrastructure development in SC-majority areas, addressing dropout rates, and promoting vocational and technical education.
*   **Enhanced Healthcare and Nutrition:** Recommending improvements in healthcare infrastructure and services in SC-majority areas, ensuring access to quality healthcare facilities, addressing malnutrition and health disparities, promoting health awareness programs, and strengthening public health systems.
*   **Housing and Basic Amenities:** Recommending programs to provide adequate housing, sanitation facilities, clean drinking water, and electricity to Scheduled Caste communities, particularly in rural areas and marginalized settlements.
*   **Social Security and Safety Nets:** Recommending expansion and strengthening of social security schemes, pension programs, and other safety nets to protect vulnerable Scheduled Caste individuals and families from poverty and economic insecurity.

**4. Fostering Socio-Economic Development and Empowerment:**

*   **Economic Empowerment and Employment:** Recommending policies and programs to promote economic empowerment of Scheduled Castes, including skill development initiatives, entrepreneurship development programs, access to credit and financial services, promotion of traditional occupations and crafts, and ensuring effective implementation of reservation policies in employment and promotions.
*   **Land Reforms and Resource Access:** Recommending effective implementation of land reforms to address historical injustices related to land ownership, ensuring access to land, forest resources, and other natural resources for Scheduled Caste communities, and promoting sustainable livelihoods.
*   **Infrastructure Development in SC Areas:** Recommending focused infrastructure development in Scheduled Caste-majority areas, including roads, irrigation facilities, communication networks, and other essential infrastructure to improve connectivity, economic opportunities, and quality of life.
*   **Financial Inclusion and Credit Access:** Recommending measures to enhance financial inclusion of Scheduled Castes, ensuring access to banking services, affordable credit, and financial literacy programs to promote economic self-reliance.
*   **Participation in Governance and Decision-Making:** Recommending measures to ensure effective participation of Scheduled Castes in governance and decision-making processes at all levels, including political representation, representation in public institutions, and inclusion in policy formulation and implementation.

**5. Monitoring, Evaluation, and Accountability:**

*   **Strengthening Monitoring Mechanisms:** Recommending the establishment or strengthening of mechanisms for regular monitoring and evaluation of the implementation of safeguards, welfare programs, and development initiatives for Scheduled Castes at all levels of government.
*   **Data Collection and Research:** Recommending improvements in data collection and research on the socio-economic conditions of Scheduled Castes to better understand their needs, challenges, and progress, and to inform policy-making.
*   **Accountability and Transparency:** Recommending measures to enhance accountability and transparency in the implementation of programs and policies for Scheduled Castes, including social audits, grievance redressal mechanisms, and ensuring responsiveness of government agencies to the needs of Scheduled Caste communities.

These recommendations can be specific and tailored to particular issues or regions, and are intended to guide the government and other stakeholders in taking concrete actions to improve the lives of Scheduled Castes and ensure their constitutional rights are fully realized.

   - **Section 121 (Criminal Conspiracy)**: This section applies to the individual who agrees to commit the crime, even if the actual theft has not yet occurred.

2. **Analysis of the Scenarios**:
   - The individual who agrees to commit the theft is guilty under Section 121 (Criminal Conspiracy) because it pertains to agreement or conspiracy to commit a crime.
   - The individual who actually commits the theft is guilty under Section 381 (Theft) as it pertains to the illegal act of taking property without consent.

3. **Conclusion**:
   - Both sections 121 and 381 are applicable, but since the question asks for the specific offence, the focus is on the conspirator. Therefore, the primary offence charged would be Section 121 (Criminal Conspiracy).

Thus, the final answer is:

\boxed{A}

instruction: Answer the following Indian legal question.
input: Discuss the provisions regarding tax treatment of income from house property under the Income Tax Act, 1961, with an example of a rented property in Kochi.
output:
**Tax Treatment of Income from House Property under the Income Tax Act, 1961: Illustrated with a Rented Property in Kochi**

**1. Provisions of the Income Tax Act, 1961, Regarding Income from House Property**

The Income Tax Act, 1961, provides specific provisions for the taxation of income derived from house property, which include both the rental income received by the landlord and the depreciation benefits available to the tenant. Here’s a structured overview:

- **Section 22:** This section deals with the taxation of income from the letting out of a house property. It covers both the rent received by the landlord and the interest on any arrears of rent, if applicable. The default tax rate applicable is 30% for individuals and 40% for companies, unless the property is under a different tax regime.

- **Section 29:** This provision allows a tenant using the property for business or profession to claim depreciation on the property. The depreciation is calculated at a standard rate (e.g., 5% per month on the cost of the building or 10% for plant and machinery).

- **Section 28:** This section allows a deduction for certain expenses made by the tenant, such as the actual rent paid (minus hotel charges if applicable) in computing the business income.

- **Section 23:** This section outlines allowable deductions for the landlord, including repairs, insurance, ground rent, etc. Capital expenditures, however, are not deductible.

- **Section 10A or 10F:** Both the landlord and tenant are required to file income tax returns, depending on their business nature.

**2. Tax Implications for Landlord and Tenant**

**Landlord (Assuming Profit-Motive):**

- **Taxable Income:** The rent received, minus allowable deductions (e.g., repairs, insurance, depreciation) is taxable under Section 22.
- **Filing:** The landlord must file an income tax return (Form 10A or 10F) if the rental income exceeds the threshold for filing.

**Tenant (Assuming Profit-Motive):**

- **Business Expense Deduction:** The rent paid (minus hotel charges) can be deducted from business income under Section 28.
- **Depreciation:** The tenant can claim depreciation on the property under Section 29, reducing taxable income.

**3. Example with a Rented Property in Kochi**

Suppose a landlord in Kochi rents out a property for Rs. 10,000 per month:

- **Landlord's Perspective:**
  - Gross Rent: Rs. 120,000 annually.
  - Deductions: Let's assume depreciation on the building is Rs. 50,000 (5% per month for 12 months).
  - Net taxable income: Rs. 70,000.
  - Tax Rate: Suppose the landlord is an individual; the taxable income falls under the 10% bracket post deduction, leading to a tax of Rs. 7,000.

- **Tenant's Perspective:**
  - Gross Rent Paid: Rs. 120,000.
  - Deductions: Rs. 120,000 (rent) minus hotel charges, say Rs. 5,000, leaving Rs. 115,000.
  - Depreciation: Say, Rs. 60,000 (5% per month for 12 months on a Rs. 1,200,000 building).
  - Net taxable income: Rs. 55,000.
  - Tax Rate: Suppose the tenant is an individual in the 20% tax bracket; the taxable income would be Rs. 55,000, leading to a tax of Rs. 11,000.

**Note:** This example is illustrative and may vary based on individual circumstances and specific deductions allowed.

**Key Considerations:**
- **Double Taxation:** The rental income at the landlord's end is taxed, and the same amount is deducted by the tenant, potentially leading to double taxation. The Act provides mechanisms to avoid this.
- **Interest on Arrears:** Interest on delayed rent payment is added to the landlord's taxable income at a rate of 9% per annum.
- **Capital Gains:** Capital gains on the sale of the property may be taxable, depending on the holding period and applicable rate.
- **Local Rental Rates:** The applicable tax rates in Kochi may influence the overall taxable income.

Both parties must carefully manage their tax obligations and deductions to optimize their tax liability while complying with the law.

instruction: Answer the following Indian legal question.
input: Explain the principle of 'Implication' in statutory interpretation. How is it applied in cases where the statute is silent on a specific issue?
output:
**Principle of Implication in Statutory Interpretation**

The principle of implication allows courts to infer additional rules or restrictions from a statute beyond what is explicitly stated. When a statute does not address a specific issue directly, courts infer the anticipated meaning from the statute's context, purpose, and relationship with existing legal principles.

**Key Aspects:**

1. **Express vs. Implied Implications:**
   - **Express Implication:** Words or context explicitly suggest a secondary rule.
   - **Implied Implication:** Courts deduce rules based on purpose, context, or related provisions.

2. **Statutory Context and Purpose:**
   - Courts evaluate the statute's broader goals and policies to determine what should be implied.
   - For example, a law prohibiting sale to minors might imply restrictions on their purchase.

3. **Plain Language Approach:**
   - Courts generally interpret statutes using common language, assuming the default allows an action unless prohibited.
   - Silence often implies permission unless counterprohibited.

4. **Case Law and Precedent:**
   - Previous decisions can shape statutory interpretation, suggesting implied meanings from similar laws.

5. **Handling Ambiguity:**
   - Ambiguous statutes require judicial determination, favoring interpretations that support the statute's effective functioning.

**Example:**
- A drug statute criminalizing possession is silent on exportation. Courts might infer exportation is illegal, aligning with the statute's control objectives.

**Conclusion:**
Implication is a judicial tool used to ensure statutes are applied coherently, even when they don’t explicitly address all scenarios. It relies on the statute's purpose and context, enabling courts to infer necessary rules for effective enforcement.

instruction: Answer the following Indian legal question.
input: What is the role of the President in determining the socially and educationally backward classes for the purposes of the Central Government?
output:
The President of India plays a significant, though not absolute, role in determining the socially and educationally backward classes for the purposes of the Central Government.  This role is primarily defined by Article 342A of the Constitution, inserted by the Constitution (One Hundred and Second Amendment) Act, 2018.

According to Article 342A(1), the President is empowered to *notify*, with respect to any State or Union Territory, the socially and educationally backward classes.  These classes, once notified, are deemed to be SEBCs for the purposes of the Constitution in relation to that specific State or Union Territory. This notification is crucial because it officially recognizes these communities as SEBCs for availing benefits and protections provided by the Central Government.

Historically, under Article 340, the President could also appoint a Commission to investigate the conditions of SEBCs and make recommendations. While Article 340 still exists, Article 342A provides a more direct mechanism for the President to act on the identification of SEBCs.  It is generally understood that the President would exercise this power on the aid and advice of the Union Council of Ministers and potentially based on recommendations from bodies like the National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC), established under Article 338B.

However, the President's role is not the final determinant. Article 342A(2) explicitly states that *Parliament* may by law provide for the inclusion in or exclusion from the *Central List* of socially and educationally backward classes notified by the President.  This signifies that while the President initiates the process of notification, Parliament retains the ultimate legislative authority to define and modify the Central List of SEBCs through law.  Furthermore, Article 342A(3) mandates that every notification issued by the President under clause (1) must be laid before each House of Parliament, ensuring parliamentary oversight.

In summary, the President's role is to *notify* SEBCs for each State and Union Territory, which is a critical step for their recognition by the Central Government. However, Parliament possesses the power to legislate and ultimately determine the Central List of SEBCs, making the process a shared responsibility with the legislative branch holding the final authority.

instruction: Answer the following Indian legal question.
input: Which articles and laws are overridden by Article 370?
output:
Article 370 did not "override" specific articles and laws in the sense of making them invalid for the rest of India. Instead, it effectively restricted the automatic application of most articles of the Indian Constitution and laws enacted by the Indian Parliament to the State of Jammu and Kashmir.

Here is a breakdown of how Article 370 impacted the application of articles and laws:

*   **Articles of the Indian Constitution:**  With the exception of Article 1 (which defines India) and Article 370 itself, and subsequently some other articles extended through Presidential Orders, the rest of the Indian Constitution was not directly applicable to Jammu and Kashmir.  For most other articles of the Constitution to apply to J&K, Presidential Orders under Article 370 were required, often with the concurrence of the State Government of J&K. This meant that articles relating to Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles of State Policy, Union-State relations, emergency provisions, and many others did not automatically extend to J&K in the same manner as they did to other states of India.  When extended, these articles were often applied with modifications or exceptions specific to J&K.

*   **Laws of the Indian Parliament:** Similarly, laws passed by the Indian Parliament did not automatically apply to Jammu and Kashmir.  Parliament's legislative power for J&K was limited.  For matters outside of Defence, Foreign Affairs, and Communications (the subjects of the Instrument of Accession), the concurrence of the State Government of J&K was needed for Parliament to legislate on subjects in the Union and Concurrent Lists. For matters in the State List, Parliament generally had no power to legislate.  To extend Indian laws to J&K, Presidential Orders under Article 370 were typically needed, again often requiring concurrence from the State Government. This meant that numerous central laws applicable across India were not in force in J&K unless specifically extended.

In essence, Article 370 created a constitutional mechanism that placed significant limitations on the reach of the Indian Constitution and Indian laws within Jammu and Kashmir, requiring specific actions (Presidential Orders and often State Government concurrence) for their application rather than automatic extension. It did not invalidate or override these articles and laws for the rest of India, but rather carved out a unique and distinct constitutional and legal relationship for Jammu and Kashmir.

instruction: Answer the following Indian legal question.
input: What are the key features of Sindhi, one of India's many regional languages?
output:
Sindhi, an Indo-Aryan language primarily spoken in the Sindh province of Pakistan and by Sindhi communities in India, possesses several key features:

*   **Indo-Aryan Language Family:** Sindhi belongs to the Indo-Aryan language family, originating from the Vracada Apabhramsa dialect of Sanskrit. This linguistic lineage connects it to other major languages of the Indian subcontinent like Hindi, Punjabi, and Gujarati.

*   **Geographical Distribution:** While its historical heartland is Sindh, Pakistan, a significant Sindhi-speaking population resides in India, particularly in states like Gujarat, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, and Madhya Pradesh, following the partition of India in 1947. This diaspora contributes to its status as a regional language in India.

*   **Writing Systems:** Sindhi is unique in employing multiple writing systems. In Pakistan and traditionally, it is written in the Perso-Arabic script, adapted to include additional letters for Sindhi specific sounds. In India, a modified Devanagari script is also officially recognized and used, particularly in educational and literary contexts. Historically, other scripts like Landa and Khudabadi were also used.

*   **Phonology:** Sindhi phonology is characterized by several distinctive features, most notably the presence of implosive consonants. It also possesses a rich set of tones and a relatively large vowel inventory compared to some other Indo-Aryan languages.

*   **Vocabulary:** Sindhi vocabulary reflects influences from various languages due to its historical and geographical location. It has borrowed extensively from Arabic and Persian, particularly in its Perso-Arabic script usage, and also retains a significant Sanskrit-derived vocabulary base, especially noticeable in its Devanagari script usage.

*   **Rich Literary and Cultural Heritage:** Sindhi boasts a vibrant literary tradition spanning centuries, encompassing Sufi poetry, folk tales, and modern literature. Figures like Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai are revered literary icons. Sindhi culture is distinct with unique customs, music, and art forms.

*   **Scheduled Language of India:** Sindhi is recognized as one of the 22 scheduled languages of India in the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution. This constitutional recognition provides it with official status and protection, promoting its development and use in various domains within India.

instruction: Answer the following Indian legal question.
input: Define and differentiate between 'bill of exchange' and 'cheque' under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. Give suitable examples.
output:
**Distinguishing Between a Bill of Exchange and a Cheque Under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881**

**1. Definition and Scope:**
   - **Bill of Exchange:** An instrument in writing, assignable to order, promising to pay a specified sum to another promptly, either immediately or at a future date. It can be drawn on any person, bank, or organization.
   - **Cheque:** A specific type of bill of exchange drawn on a bank or other financial institution. It is an order to a bank to pay a certain amount from the drawer's account.

**2. Payable Options:**
   - **Bill of Exchange:** Can be payable immediately (at sight) or at a future date, with a typically limited term (e.g., up to 6 months).
   - **Cheque:** Primarily payable on demand, though future-dated cheques (e.g., 30, 60 days) also exist.

**3. Negotiability and Transferability:**
   - Both bills and cheques are negotiable, meaning they can be transferred.
   - Cheques can be discounted at a bank for a small fee, while bills can be discounted through bill brokers.

**4. Legal Standing and Liabilities:**
   - Under the Negotiable Instruments Act, banks are liable for honoured cheques, even if the drawer defaults.
   - Bills can be more complex, with dishhonour rules and potential interest accrual if drawn with a future date.

**5. Examples:**
   - **Bill of Exchange:** A contractor sends a bill to a client, which the client endorses and presents to the bank.
   - **Cheque:** A utility company sends a cheque to a customer for payment.

**6. Additional Considerations:**
   - **Crossing:** Cheques can be crossed, specifying a payee, while bills are typically simple instruments.
   - **Interest Accrual:** Future-dated bills can accrue interest, while cheques generally do not unless specifically stated.

**Conclusion:**
A bill of exchange is versatile, applicable to various payees, while a cheque is a specialized bill drawn on a banking institution. Both are crucial in financial transactions, facilitating Smooth fund transfers and Payments.

instruction: Answer the following Indian legal question.
input: How are the provisions of article 239B applied in relation to the National Capital Territory, the Lieutenant Governor and the Legislative Assembly?
output:
Article 239B of the Indian Constitution empowers the Lieutenant Governor (LG) of the National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi to promulgate Ordinances when the Legislative Assembly of Delhi is not in session. This power mirrors that of the President at the Union level and Governors at the State level.

Specifically, the application in relation to the NCT, the LG, and the Legislative Assembly is as follows:

1.  **Lieutenant Governor as the Authority:** As the Administrator of the NCT of Delhi (designated under Article 239AA), the LG is the authority vested with the power to promulgate Ordinances under Article 239B.

2.  **Conditions for Promulgation:** The LG can promulgate an Ordinance only when the Legislative Assembly is not in session.  Additionally, the LG must be satisfied that circumstances exist which render it necessary for them to take immediate action. This satisfaction is based on their assessment of the situation.

3.  **Scope of Ordinances:** The Ordinance-making power of the LG extends to matters concerning which the Legislative Assembly has the power to make laws. However, this power is subject to the legislative competence of the Delhi Assembly as defined by the Constitution.

4.  **Laying before the Legislative Assembly:** Every Ordinance promulgated under Article 239B must be laid before the Legislative Assembly of Delhi as soon as may be after its reassembly.

5.  **Duration and Cessation of Ordinances:** An Ordinance promulgated under Article 239B ceases to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the date of the reassembly of the Legislative Assembly, or if, before the expiration of that period, a resolution disapproving it is passed by the Legislative Assembly and agreed to by the Lieutenant Governor, or if the Ordinance is withdrawn by the Lieutenant Governor.  Therefore, the Legislative Assembly has a check on the LG's ordinance-making power through the possibility of disapproval.

6.  **Relationship with Council of Ministers:** While Article 239B grants the LG ordinance-making power, the exercise of this power in relation to matters within the purview of the Legislative Assembly and the elected government in Delhi is subject to the broader constitutional framework governing Delhi.  The LG is generally expected to act on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers in matters where the Legislative Assembly has legislative powers, except in matters where the LG is required to act in their discretion by or under any law.  While the exact scope of discretionary powers has been subject to judicial interpretation and legislative amendments, the ordinance-making power is generally considered to be exercised within the framework of the constitutional scheme for Delhi, including the role of the elected government.

In summary, Article 239B provides the LG of Delhi with the power to legislate by ordinance when the Assembly is not in session, subject to legislative oversight by the Delhi Legislative Assembly and within the broader constitutional context of the NCT of Delhi's governance.

instruction: Answer the following Indian legal question.
input: What does article 219 stipulate about an oath or affirmation by Judges of High Courts before they enter upon their office?
output: Article 219 of the Indian Constitution stipulates that every person appointed to be a Judge of a High Court must, before entering upon their office, make and subscribe to an oath or affirmation. This oath or affirmation is to be taken before the Governor of the State or some person appointed by the Governor for that purpose.  The form of the oath or affirmation is prescribed in the Third Schedule of the Constitution.  Specifically, as per Form VIII in the Third Schedule for Judges of a High Court, the oath or affirmation requires the Judge to swear (or affirm) that they will: bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution of India as by law established; uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India; duly and faithfully and to the best of their ability, knowledge, and judgment perform the duties of their office without fear or favour, affection or ill-will; and uphold the Constitution and the laws.  Therefore, Article 219 mandates the taking of an oath or affirmation in the form detailed in the Third Schedule before a High Court Judge can assume their office, and specifies who administers this oath.

instruction: Answer the following Indian legal question.
input: Discuss the concept of 'specific performance of reciprocal promises' under the Specific Relief Act, with an example related to joint ventures in the renewable energy sector in Gujarat.
output:
### Discussion on 'Specific Performance of Reciprocal Promises' under the Specific Relief Act

The concept of "specific performance of reciprocal promises" under the **Specific Relief Act, 1963** is a crucial aspect of enforcing contractual obligations where parties have made reciprocal commitments, i.e., each party promises to do something in exchange for the other's performance. Specific performance is an equitable remedy that compels one party to fulfill its obligations under a contract, even if the performance is not immediately due or if the benefit to the other party is not immediate or direct.

Under the Specific Relief Act, specific performance can be granted if:

1. **The contract is enforceable in law or equity**: The contract must satisfy the basic requirements of a valid contract (e.g., offer, acceptance, consideration).
2. **There is a legal or equitable right to the relief**: The court must be satisfied that the specific performance is appropriate and just.
3. **Specific performance is fair and equitable (just and appropriate)**: The remedy must be tailored to the circumstances of the case.
4. **The court has the power to enforce specific performance**: The court must have the necessary authority or jurisdiction to order specific performance.

In the context of a **joint venture** in the renewable energy sector in Gujarat, specific performance of reciprocal promises can be illustrated as follows:

#### Example:
- **Parties Involved**: 
  - **A** and **B** enter into a joint venture agreement to develop a renewable energy project in Gujarat.
  - Under the agreement, **A** promises to contribute capital and technological expertise, while **B** agrees to provide project management and expertise in renewable energy solutions.

- **Reciprocal Promises**:
  - **A** and **B** each agree to fulfill their obligations as per the terms of the joint venture agreement.
  - The project involves the deployment of solar energy solutions, and both parties are bound to contribute equally or proportionally as per the agreement.

- **Breach of Reciprocal Promise**:
  - Suppose **A** fails to contribute the agreed capital or expertise on time, causing delays in the project's execution.
  - **B** has fulfilled their obligations but suffers losses due to the delayed project timelines.

- **Application of Specific Performance**:
  - **B** may approach the court to seek specific performance, compelling **A** to fulfill its contractual obligations within a reasonable timeframe.
- **Court's Role**:
  - The court will examine whether specific performance is just and appropriate. For instance, if **A** has already significantly breached the contract (e.g., failed to contribute any capital or expertise), the court may decline to order specific performance, as it may no longer be fair or equitable.
  - However, if **A**'s breach is minor or technical, and the contract stipulates reciprocal promises, the court may order specific performance, forcing **A** to perform its obligations to allow the joint venture to proceed as intended.

### Conclusion:
The concept of specific performance of reciprocal promises under the Specific Relief Act is a powerful tool for enforcing contractual obligations in collaborations such as joint ventures. In the renewable energy sector, where projects require significant investments and expertise, specific performance ensures that parties fulfill their commitments, ensuring the success of the joint venture and promoting trust among collaborators. Courts, however, exercise caution in granting specific performance, ensuring that it remains a just and equitable remedy in the circumstances.
